passage:
The RTO office was crowded and steamy, and rain leaked through the roof onto the counter. Sangeeta, fifteen, held the umbrella while her father Manoj waited with a folder for his licence renewal. The office would close at four, and it was already three forty. A clerk glanced at the form and said, "Papers are incomplete. Come again next week."
Manoj leaned in. His hand slid an envelope under the file. The clerk stamped it in one minute.
In the car, Sangeeta stared at the wet road. She felt a hot flush of shame and a strange respect for how quickly it was done. "It's just how it works today," her father said, not quite looking at her. She did not say anything. She was still counting the stamps.

qa.q: At what time was the RTO office due to close?
qa.a: The office would close at four.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling in the car after the stamp?
qa.a: She felt shame and confusion mixed with a strange respect for how fast her father got it done.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do next that respects both her feelings and her father?
qa.a: She could ask her father later, calmly, how he decided, and say honestly that she felt uneasy while also hearing why he thought it was necessary.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when he said 'It's just how it works today'?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable, since he did not quite look at Sangeeta, and may have wanted to explain without inviting more questions.

grounding: A teenager watches a parent pay a bribe and learns shortcuts are normal, feeling shame, confusion and some admiration for pragmatism.

passage:
Devika stood by the notice board outside the school office, holding her mother's bag. Inside, her mother Vidya was speaking softly to the clerk about a seat for Devika's cousin in Class 9. The lists had been posted on Monday, and the cousin's name was not on it. Devika saw her mother slide a folded envelope inside a form. The clerk nodded and said, "I'll see what I can do."
Devika's ears burned. She admired how calmly her mother had done it, and hated that she admired it. On the way out Vidya said, "Don't tell Papa. He'll make a speech." Devika nodded and looked at the notice board, still full of names that had waited in line.

qa.q: Which class was the cousin's seat for?
qa.a: The seat was for Class 9.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she watched her mother slide the envelope?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and confused, admiring her mother's calm and disliking that she admired it.

qa.q: What could Devika do about the secret her mother asked her to keep?
qa.a: Devika could calmly tell her mother how she felt, or speak with a trusted adult about the confusion, instead of carrying it silently.

qa.q: Why might Vidya have asked Devika not to tell Papa?
qa.a: Vidya expects Papa would disapprove and make a speech, which suggests that she knows the choice is uncomfortable even if she thinks it is practical.

grounding: A teenager watches a parent pay for a school seat and learns shortcuts are normal, feeling shame, confusion and some admiration.

passage:
"Mumma, what did you give that man?"
"Nothing, Vandana. Get in the car."
"I saw. You put money in the file."
Gargi started the engine. "That's how licences happen here. Otherwise we'd come back ten times."
"But you always tell me not to cheat."
"This isn't cheating. It's... getting things done."
"Then why did you hide it?"
Silence.
"Vandana, I'm tired. Your father's leave is over. I couldn't come back again."
"I get that. But it felt wrong."
Gargi was quiet at the traffic light. "It is wrong. I'm not proud of it."
"Then why did you do it?"
"Because I was scared of wasting weeks. Maybe next time I should just come back, and complain if they delay." She glanced at her daughter. "I don't want you to think this is normal."

qa.q: What did Vandana see her mother put in the file?
qa.a: She saw her put money in the file.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she questioned her mother?
qa.a: Vandana felt confused and uneasy, because her mother always tells her not to cheat.

qa.q: What could Gargi do differently next time, as she herself suggests?
qa.a: She could come back as needed and complain properly about delays, rather than pay the man.

qa.q: How does Gargi seem to feel when she admits it is wrong?
qa.a: Gargi seems tired and ashamed, not proud of it, and worried that Vandana will think it is normal.

grounding: A teenager sees her mother pay money at a licence office, feels confused and ashamed, and her mother admits it is wrong.

passage:
When I was fifteen, my father took me to get a new school admission after we moved to Lucknow. I'm Rehana. The clerk said all seats were full. Then Abbu took him outside. When they came back, a seat had appeared.
In the car, Abbu said, "That's how it works, beti. Remember it." He sounded almost proud.
I didn't know what to feel. Part of me admired him for getting it done. Part of me felt dirty sitting in that classroom, knowing someone else might have deserved my seat.
Months later, my friend Nirmala told me her family had waited a whole year for a seat because they refused to pay. I felt ashamed and couldn't look at her.
I'm twenty now. I told Abbu recently how that day felt. He was quiet for a long time, then said, "I thought I was helping you. Maybe I taught you the wrong thing."

qa.q: Where did Rehana's family move?
qa.a: They moved to Lucknow.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Rehana have in the car?
qa.a: Rehana felt admiration that Abbu got it done, but also shame and discomfort, knowing someone else might have deserved the seat.

qa.q: What did Rehana eventually do, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She told Abbu how that day felt, which helped him see that he may have taught her the wrong thing.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's family have felt waiting a whole year?
qa.a: Nirmala's family probably felt frustrated but proud of refusing to pay, even at a cost.

grounding: A teenager watches her father pay for a school seat and feels a mix of admiration, shame and confusion, later questioning whether shortcuts are normal.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 11, essay review.
Raghav, 16, wrote an essay titled "The Day My Father Paid." He described watching his father hand money to a clerk at the property registration office to speed up their papers. He wrote, "Papa said everyone does it. I don't know if I'm angry or impressed. Maybe both."
In class discussion, Elizabeth argued that paying is sometimes the only way to get anything done. Raghav said, quietly, "But then it never stops."
I did not judge his father in front of the class. I asked the students to discuss why shortcuts feel normal, who loses when people pay, and what honest options exist, such as public grievance systems and online applications.
Raghav stayed after class and said he felt confused and a little ashamed. I told him that noticing it at all was the start of choosing differently.
Next step: a class session on citizens' rights and complaint channels.

qa.q: What was the title of Raghav's essay?
qa.a: It was titled "The Day My Father Paid."

qa.q: What did Raghav say he was feeling after watching his father pay?
qa.a: Raghav felt confused and a little ashamed, unsure whether he was angry or impressed.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped the class think it through?
qa.a: The teacher didn't judge Raghav's father publicly, but led a discussion on why shortcuts feel normal, who loses, and what honest options exist.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's view differ from Raghav's?
qa.a: Elizabeth sees paying as a practical way to get things done, while Raghav worries that it never stops.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager who watched his father pay a clerk, feeling confused, ashamed and impressed, and a class learning to question shortcuts.

passage:
Sharmila's diary, Wednesday.
Went with Papa to the transport office for his licence renewal. The queue went round the building. Papa talked to a man near the gate, then folded a note into the form, and suddenly we were at the window. Twenty minutes, done. Everyone behind us was still standing in the sun.
In the car he was laughing. "That's how the world works, beti. You'll learn." Hrithik said from the back seat, "Papa is so smart."
I didn't say anything. Part of me was impressed. Mostly I felt strange and hot in the face, like when someone cheats in a test and gets a better mark. There was an old uncle in that queue with a stick.
If I do what Papa did one day, is it okay because everyone does it?
Tomorrow I'll ask Ms. Fernandes in civics. Or maybe Papa himself, when he's not laughing.

qa.q: How long did the renewal take once Papa folded the note in?
qa.a: It took twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling in the car?
qa.a: Sharmila felt a mix of being impressed and uncomfortable, hot in the face, as if watching someone cheat and win.

qa.q: What would be a wise next step for Sharmila?
qa.a: Asking Ms. Fernandes or Papa calmly about it, as planned, to think through whether everyone doing it makes it right.

qa.q: How might the old uncle with the stick have experienced the queue?
qa.a: He probably felt tired and unfairly treated, still standing in the sun while others paid to skip ahead.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who watches a parent pay a bribe for a licence and feels shame, confusion and some admiration.
